slides.title: Version 0.1, set in stone
slides.say:
STORY (2009-01-08): Five days after the genesis block, Satoshi announced Bitcoin version 0.1 - a Windows program on SourceForge. A year and a half later he wrote the sentence this course keeps returning to: once version 0.1 was released, the core design was set in stone for the rest of its lifetime. Everything this chapter builds, configures and queries descends from that one program, which is why Bitcoin Core is called the reference implementation.
SOURCE: Announcement of 2009-01-08 on the metzdowd.com cryptography list ('Bitcoin v0.1 released'); the 'set in stone' sentence is Satoshi's forum post of 2010-06-17; project history summarized at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Core.
IMAGE: the 0.5.2 GUI (MIT licence) - the same program two years on.
slides.concept: The software came first - the program IS the specification

slides.title: One program, many postures
slides.say:
SAY: A pruned node is a full node that deletes old block files after it has verified them, so that it needs far less disk space.
ASK: Which posture still enforces every consensus rule? (both - that is the point)
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - PrunedNode, InitialDownload.
slides.concept: Same rules, different storage - pruning keeps the checks, drops the history

slides.title: From source to binary
slides.say:
SAY: The build branch is about turning the text of Bitcoin Core into a program that can run. The book calls this part of the chapter the Bitcoin development environment: the tools, libraries and support software a developer needs for writing Bitcoin applications, which the chapter walks through step by step.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - Build.
slides.concept: Trust arithmetic, not downloads

slides.title: Clone it, then pick your version by tag
slides.say:
SAY: Git is a distributed version control system, and a repository is the database in which it keeps a project and all of its history. The book calls Git the most widely used distributed version control system and an essential part of the toolkit of every software developer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Why does the course pin a commit instead of saying 'latest'?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - GitRepository, ReleaseTag.
slides.concept: A release is a tag; a tag names one exact snapshot

slides.title: Dozens of builders, one identical binary
slides.say:
STORY (since 2011; Guix from release 22.0): A downloaded binary asks for trust; Bitcoin Core answers with arithmetic. Every release is built reproducibly - first under Gitian, since release 22.0 under Guix - so that anyone compiling the tagged source gets a byte-identical result. Independent builders publish signed hashes of what they produced, side by side, in a public repository. If one build differed, its hash would betray it instantly - the same trick the chapter's Merkle root plays on transactions.
SOURCE: bitcoin-core/guix.sigs on GitHub: per-release folders of builder attestations; Guix build documentation in the pinned source tree, contrib/guix/README.md.
slides.concept: Verify, don't trust - applied to the software itself

slides.title: From source to bitcoind
slides.say:
SAY: CMake is the build system that Bitcoin Core has used since release 29.0. The manual of CMake explains its role: a buildsystem describes how to build a project's executables and libraries from its source code using a build tool to automate the process, and CMake lets a project describe its buildsystem abstractly in files written in the CMake language, from which it generates a preferred buildsystem for each user (Kitware, 2026).
ASK: Why does the project treat review and tests as the bottleneck?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - CMakeBuild, SoftwareTesting.
slides.concept: The build system turns audited text into your node

slides.title: Running and talking to it
slides.say:
SAY: Operation is the second large part of the chapter, and it is about what happens after the software has been built or downloaded: how a node is started, how it is configured, how its state is observed, and what kind of wallet comes with it.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - Operation.
slides.concept: A daemon, a log that explains itself, and one protocol

slides.title: The log narrates everything the node decides
slides.say:
SAY: The start-up log is the stream of messages that the node writes while it starts, and afterwards as it runs. With the option that sends the log to the console it appears in the terminal, and otherwise it goes to a file called debug.log in the data directory, as the documentation of the data directory states (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
ASK: Where would you look first when a node misbehaves? (the answer is this slide's title)
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - StartupLog, Daemon.
slides.concept: When a node misbehaves, the log already wrote the diagnosis

slides.title: The project that outlives its keyholders
slides.say:
STORY (2011 and 2014): Bitcoin Core is the program Satoshi published in January 2009, still developed in public. In 2011 Satoshi handed the project to Gavin Andresen - the faucet builder of chapter 2 - and withdrew. In April 2014 Andresen passed the lead-maintainer role to Wladimir van der Laan to focus on protocol work. Hundreds of contributors and several maintainers later, the repository, its tags and its releases carry on; no single person has been indispensable since.
SOURCE: Repository history of bitcoin/bitcoin (the chapter's pinned checkout is commit 05bc2f53); maintainer handoffs of 2011 and April 2014 as recorded in the project history and summarized at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Core.
slides.concept: Maintainers change; the repository and its rules remain

slides.title: Talking to the node: bitcoin-cli and JSON-RPC
slides.say:
SAY: JSON-RPC is a protocol for remote procedure calls whose messages are written in JSON. Its specification describes it as a stateless, light-weight remote procedure call protocol that defines a few data structures and the rules for processing them, independent of the transport, so that the same messages may travel within a process, over sockets or over HTTP (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013).
ASK: Your phone wallet never shows this - what is it speaking underneath?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - JsonRpc, BitcoinCommand.
slides.concept: Every GUI and every explorer speaks this same protocol

slides.title: Wallets are descriptors now
slides.say:
SAY: A descriptor wallet is a wallet whose content is a set of output descriptions, each stating one family of scripts that the wallet can receive to and spend from. Bitcoin Core's documentation says that its code internally stores and operates on descriptors to reason about the sets of outputs that belong to the wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
ASK: What does the # suffix buy you when you mistype one character?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - DescriptorWallet, LegacyWallet.
slides.concept: A descriptor states, in one line, what the wallet watches

slides.title: Decode a real transaction
slides.say:
SAY: A decoded transaction is the structure that results from reading the bytes of a serialized transaction and naming each field. The command decoderawtransaction takes the hexadecimal string and returns a JSON object (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Which of the two identifiers survives a witness change, and why does that matter?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - DecodedTransaction, TransactionIdentifier.
slides.concept: The node explains any transaction - Alice's included

slides.say:
SAY: The data branch is about what a node holds and what the interface shows of it: the transactions that move value, the blocks that gather them into the shared record, and the state of the chain that results.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - Data.
slides.concept: Headers, roots, and the same node from your own code

slides.title: The header is 80 bytes of commitment
slides.say:
SAY: The block header is the summary at the head of every block.
ASK: Chapter 2 drew this tree with toy leaves - what changed here? (nothing but the data)
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - BlockHeader, MerkleRoot.
slides.concept: Eighty bytes pin megabytes - that is the whole trick

slides.title: The chapter as data, and in one library call
slides.say:
SAY: The semantics branch connects the chapter to the course's wider theme, the meaning of data. A node answers every request in the JSON text format, a structure of names and values, which a program can read but whose names carry no meaning of their own; the field called height in a block's answer means what the documentation says it means, and nothing in the text states it.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 3 - Semantics.
slides.concept: The course page and your scripts read the same node
